Cuando llegamos, ya se había ido

To choose between pretérito perfecto and indefinido according to the time period (hoy, este verano / ayer, el verano pasado).
To use imperfecto for the background, habits and interrupted actions, and indefinido for events.

September. The first class of the B2 group at the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest. Costel, the lorry driver who passed B1 in June, arrived first. Doamna Ecaterina, the former translator, has come “just to listen”. Ana has just come back from a whole summer in Madrid.
Teacher! How was the summer? Did Mihai learn to make the tortilla?
It’s been a very long summer for him. On the first day, the tortilla fell on the floor when he was trying to flip it.
And your mother, Señora Carmen, what did she do?
Nothing. She had seen that disaster many times before. My father used to do the same when he was young.
Well, this summer I’ve made twelve trips to Germany and I haven’t cooked a single egg.
And have you studied anything, Costel?
A bit. While I was driving, I listened to podcasts in Spanish. One night, near Munich, I realised I understood almost everything.
That’s the most wonderful thing. I was your age when I started translating novels. By then, I had already lived in Madrid for ten years.
Ten years? I didn’t know. Why did you come back to Romania?
That’s a long story. I’ll tell you another day, when you know how to use the pluperfect properly.
(laughing) Then that’s where we’ll start today. Open your books: “When we arrived, he had already left.”
“ya había visto” = she had already seen
The accent changes the tense: «hablo» (present) versus «habló» (indefinido); «canto» versus «cantó». Listen for the written accent!
«a-BÍ-a» has three syllables; «había hecho» runs together: [a-bia-É-cho].
Stress on the last syllable: sar-TÉN.
In Spain, the choice depends on the time period the action belongs to:
a period still open: hoy, esta semana, este verano, este año
a finished period: ayer, la semana pasada, el verano pasado, en 2020
experiences with no date: ¿Has estado en Japón?
a dated event: Estuve en Japón en 2019.
Este verano he hecho doce viajes.
El verano pasado hice doce viajes.
In Latin America and in north-western Spain the indefinido is used much more often, even with “hoy”. In the DELE exam both are accepted, as long as you are consistent.
2. Imperfecto and indefinido in the same story
The imperfect paints the background, the indefinido moves the story forward:
event: De repente, sonó el teléfono.
habit: Mi padre solía cocinar los domingos.
a single time: Un domingo cocinó para veinte personas.
the action that interrupts it: …me di cuenta de que lo entendía todo.

The typical mistake: “Ayer estaba en el cine” for a finished action. Correct: “Ayer estuve en el cine”. The imperfect would mean something else is about to happen (“Ayer estaba en el cine cuando me llamaste”).
3. Pluscuamperfecto: the past of the past
The imperfect of haber (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían) + participle. It shows that an action was already finished before another one in the past:
When we arrived, he had already left.
My mother had seen that disaster many times before.
I had never eaten such a good tortilla.
Words that often call for the pluscuamperfecto: ya, todavía no, nunca antes, para entonces.
4. Soler in the imperfect and the pretérito anterior
“Soler” + infinitive expresses a habit. In the past it is used almost only in the imperfect: solía, solías, solía, solíamos, solíais, solían.
When I was little, I usually spent the summers in the village.
The pretérito anterior (hube, hubiste, hubo… + participle) only appears in literature, after “apenas, en cuanto, cuando”. You only need to recognise it; in speech it is replaced by the indefinido.
As soon as he had finished dinner, he went to bed.
“I went to the cinema yesterday.” (finished action)
Ayer he estado en el cine.
As soon as he had finished
“I had never eaten anything like that.”
While I was driving, I listened to podcasts.
¿Qué le pasó a Mihai el primer día?
La tortilla se le cayó al suelo
¿Cuántos viajes ha hecho Costel este verano?
¿Cuántos años había vivido Ecaterina en Madrid?

When Ana, Mihai and Rosa Elena arrived in Madrid on the first day of July, it was forty degrees in the shade. Señora Carmen, Ana’s mother, was waiting for them at the door of her flat in Lavapiés with a fan in one hand and a frying pan in the other. Ana laughed. Mihai didn’t. He had understood the message perfectly.

In May, in the garden in Bucharest, Ana had set a condition for staying in Romania: they would spend the summers in Madrid and Mihai would finally learn to make a decent potato tortilla. Mihai had said “deal” without thinking much about it. Now, in front of that heavy black frying pan, he was beginning to regret it.

The first lesson began the next day, at ten in the morning, before the heat became unbearable. Carmen usually cooked early, like her mother and grandmother before her. She put on the table six eggs, four potatoes, an onion, olive oil and salt. Nothing else.
“With onion?” asked Mihai, who had read on the internet that this was a delicate subject.

“In this house, always with onion,” Carmen replied very seriously. “My mother made it with onion, I make it with onion and Ana will make it with onion. If one day you want to make it without onion, you go back to Bucharest.”

Mihai was a doctor. He had operated on hearts, stitched wounds at three in the morning and saved lives. But never, in his whole life, had he had to flip a tortilla. The first attempt ended up on the kitchen floor. The second, on the worktop. The third, on Mihai’s T-shirt; he had to go and shower while Carmen cleaned up without saying a word.
When he came back, Carmen had made another tortilla, perfect, golden and round like a moon. Rosa Elena was eating it with her hands.

“Never mind,” said Carmen. “Your father-in-law, my Juan, dropped about fifty on the floor before he made his first good one. And even today, if I don’t keep an eye on him, he drops one now and then.” From the living room, Juan protested without taking his eyes off the football.

That night, while Carmen was asleep, Juan called Mihai out onto the terrace. He poured him a glass of wine and, lowering his voice like someone confessing a crime, told him the truth: in forty-five years of marriage, he had never managed to flip a tortilla without breaking it. He always started it, and Carmen always finished it. “I’ve been pretending for half my life,” he said. “Don’t you make the same mistake. Learn properly.”

Mihai promised him he would learn. They clinked glasses in silence, looking at the rooftops of Lavapiés, while down in the street some neighbours were arguing loudly about football. For the first time since they had known each other, Mihai felt that he and his father-in-law shared more than their love for Ana: they shared a fear, and that fear was a frying pan.

All through July, Mihai practised every morning. While Ana caught up with her lifelong friends and Rosa Elena discovered the fountains of the Retiro, he peeled potatoes, chopped onions and cried, sometimes because of the onion and sometimes out of despair. Carmen watched him from a chair, with her fan, and spoke only to give orders: “More heat.” “Less heat.” “Don’t touch it.” “Now.”

One afternoon, Elena video-called from Bucharest. She saw her son in a flowery apron, his face covered in flour and his eyes red from the onion, and for a moment she was speechless. Then she burst out laughing so hard that she had to sit down. “I’ve never seen you like this in your whole life,” she said. “If your grandfather could see you…” Carmen came up to the screen and the two mothers talked for half an hour, each in her own language, with Ana translating, about how hard it was to train the men of the family.

Some nights, when everyone was asleep, Mihai got up quietly and practised the wrist movement with a plate and a saucepan lid, over and over, like a surgeon rehearsing a difficult operation. On one of those nights, Ana found him in the kitchen at two in the morning, in his underpants, flipping an empty lid. She said nothing. She went back to bed and laughed silently into her pillow for ten minutes.

Little by little, the tortillas stopped falling. At first they came out burnt. Then raw in the middle. One day at the end of July, one came out that was neither burnt nor raw. Carmen tasted it in silence, chewing slowly, like a judge on a TV show. Then she put her fork down on the table.
Mihai had never received such a moving compliment.

Rosa Elena, meanwhile, had decided that she wanted to learn too. Carmen gave her a bowl, a fork and two eggs, and the little girl beat them so energetically that half of it ended up on the walls. “That’s how your mother started,” Carmen told her, patiently wiping the wall. “Exactly the same. She was your age and she had tortilla coming out of her ears.” Ana, from the doorway, swore she didn’t remember any of it.

The final exam came in mid-August. Lucía and Javier, Ana’s lifelong friends, had organised a dinner on their terrace to say goodbye before the family went back to Bucharest. Each guest had to bring a dish. Ana, without consulting anyone, had announced in the friends’ group chat: “Mihai is bringing the tortilla.”

Mihai didn’t sleep that night. At seven in the morning he was already in the kitchen. Carmen appeared in her dressing gown, looked at him and, instead of sitting down with her fan, stood beside him. Without a word, she opened a high cupboard and took out a small, old frying pan, its wooden handle worn by the years.
“It was my grandmother’s,” she said. “I learnt with this pan. Juan learnt with this pan. And I taught Ana with this pan, though she says she doesn’t remember.”

That morning’s tortilla wasn’t perfect. It was a bit lopsided on one side and had a small crack in the middle. But it was golden on the outside, juicy on the inside, and when Mihai flipped it with a quick flick of the wrist, it landed exactly on the plate. Rosa Elena clapped. Carmen said nothing, but Mihai saw that she was smiling.

That evening, on Lucía and Javier’s terrace, the tortilla disappeared in five minutes. Javier, who considered himself an expert, asked for the recipe. Lucía asked if it was Carmen’s. Ana proudly said no: her husband had made it, the Romanian doctor, the same man who in July couldn’t even peel a potato.

Javier, who was from Valladolid, spent half an hour defending tortilla without onion, with arguments that seemed to come straight out of a political debate. Lucía, who was from Buenos Aires, replied that in Argentina the potato tortilla always had onion, and that without onion it was just a fried egg with potatoes. The other guests split into two camps. Rosa Elena, who didn’t understand the argument, calmly ate the last piece.
“With onion or without onion?” someone asked from the back.
Mihai looked at Carmen, who was sitting in a corner with her fan, and answered without hesitating:

Two weeks later, at Barajas airport, Carmen gave Mihai a tightly tied cloth bag. She asked him not to open it until he got to Bucharest. Mihai obeyed. When he finally opened it, in the kitchen of their house, by the window overlooking the little walnut tree, he found inside the grandmother’s old frying pan, wrapped in a tea towel, and a handwritten note in shaky letters.
“For Mihai, who has learnt. Now it’s yours. When Rosa Elena grows up, it will be her turn. With onion. Carmen.”

That same evening, Mihai called Carmen to thank her. He struggled to find the words, because in Spanish he still got nervous when he wanted to say something important. In the end he just said that he would look after it. Carmen was silent for a few seconds. Then she told him that her grandmother had brought that pan from her village in Extremadura in 1950, in a cardboard suitcase, when she went to Madrid to work as a maid in a house, without knowing anyone, at fifteen.
“She left home and went far away too,” said Carmen. “And she put down roots too. That’s why I’m giving it to you, son. Because you’re one of those who stay.”

Mihai hung the frying pan on the kitchen wall, next to the photo of the three soldiers and Vasile’s ring. Ana watched him from the doorway. He turned round and said to her, very seriously: “Tomorrow I’m making dinner.” Rosa Elena shouted from the living room: “With onion!”

Costel writes in the club’s group chat about his summer.
This summer I’ve spent more time in the lorry than at home. I’ve made twelve trips to Germany and two to Italy.
The nicest trip was the one in August. I was heading for Verona when I saw a sign: “Valencia, 1,200 km”. I thought of Álex and almost turned the steering wheel.

In the end I didn’t go, of course. But that night I called him and told him that, when I was his age, I used to dream of driving lorries. He told me that now he dreams of being a Spanish teacher. Like Ana.
